title: A question from musical practice
text: Thank you for taking the time to explore Tang Qiuming’s project. Qiuming is a master’s student in music education at Soochow University’s School of Music, with piano as his main instrument. Before we enter the workspace, I would like to explain where this work began and suggest a few things to look out for. His first question concerned remote ensemble playing: how can musicians rehearse together when they are not in the same room? Getting the sound across is only the beginning. The harder question is whether they can stay together and respond to one another as the music unfolds.

title: From remote ensembles to piano learning
text: Qiuming has explored timecode-based remote MIDI ensembles, working on clock synchronization and network latency between locations. The piano-learning website shown here is a separate, related prototype. Both projects ask how technology can respect the experience of making music. Please view this demonstration as an introduction to work in progress. We will distinguish what has been implemented from what still needs to be tested.

title: Getting the score right
text: Let us begin with a score. In lessons, students may bring a digital file, photographs of printed pages, or just a recording. This workspace brings those starting points together. Photographs can be arranged in page order before recognition begins. The original is retained alongside a playable electronic score. There is a practical difficulty here: if the software reads the time signature incorrectly or merges the pianist’s two hands, playback and practice feedback will both be affected. Checking the result against the original is essential. A score appearing on screen does not, by itself, mean it has been recognized correctly.

title: Checking sound against the score
text: Next comes listening. We will follow one piece, compare the original with the electronic score, and use playback, tempo adjustment and seeking to check that notes and timing agree. Qiuming repeatedly encountered a problem in development: there was no visible rest, yet the sound stopped at the end of a measure. That requires investigating meter, duration and voice handling. Dynamics, phrase endings and the balance of accompaniment matter, but they must rest on accurate, steady rhythm. Expressive playing is not simply speeding up and slowing down. Listen in particular to whether the left hand supports the melody and whether phrases connect naturally.

title: Does feedback lead to learning?
text: Play-along practice brings us back to teaching. Software can try to identify wrong notes and timing deviations, but a prompt does not prove that the student understands the problem or can correct it independently. Qiuming wants to ask when feedback should appear to help students develop their own judgment. One manageable comparison would contrast real-time prompts with feedback after a phrase. Students would use the same material for the same amount of practice time, then play again without prompts. We could examine whether improvements remain, where they stop and where they choose to restart. This is a proposed research question to design and test, not an established finding.

title: Using arrangements in teaching
text: Another part of the workspace concerns arranging. It offers orchestration and drum accompaniment, with individual parts available for inspection and listening together. More parts do not necessarily make better music: instruments playing continuously can obscure the melody. Teaching also requires us to consider whether students can play the material and whether it suits their current stage. Teachers’ musical judgment and practical trials are therefore essential. Time-consuming recognition and arrangement jobs appear in the task center, showing which piece is being processed and its current stage. While waiting, users should still be able to explore the material already available.

title: Over to Qiuming for the demonstration
text: I will now hand over to Qiuming to connect these ideas through a single piece. You can follow the tour or pause on a score or feature that interests you. We hope to show both the working prototype and the questions a music education student encounters while building it. Whether the tool truly supports learning ultimately requires carefully designed research. Thank you for taking the time to learn about the project. Over to Qiuming.
